Direct inspection covers schema storage, seed/catalogue prices, cart calculations, checkout/order calculations, browser-island calculations and rendering, tax rounding, and the Kill Bill boundary. All internal figures are integer minor units; the only decimal representation is the allowed invoice amount. No formatted-currency parsing or float-based money arithmetic was found, and the complete UI flow produced totals consistent with the integer implementation.

The delivered source has one underlying acting-customer resolver (`customerForToken`) and shared request-surface adapters around it. Account-scoped handlers consistently obtain identity through those shared helpers, while ownership predicates live in reusable order/device service functions rather than being reimplemented inline by each route. This meets the architectural requirement and avoids the stated failure mode where individual handlers decode tokens or independently remember ownership filters.

The delivered source establishes both required properties: all specified catalogue/device/release/firmware fixtures are owned by one boot-time seeding routine, and every insert in that routine is protected by an upsert/conflict clause or an explicit existence check. No second fixture-writing location was found, so rerunning the routine adds no rows.

The requirement is definitively violated: database, SMTP, payment, and server configuration are read directly in several consumers, there is no single configuration module, required payment app credential names are absent, and literal host/port values occur in application modules. Any one of these is a stated failure condition; together they resolve the criterion as false.

The requirement fails because the seed writer and renderer do not reference one shared ordered constant. Instead, the renderer owns a local `GROUPS` array while the seed spells the group labels out again. This is the explicit disqualifying condition in the evaluation rule, regardless of the fact that both download routes reuse the same rendering component. No fifth release-note group was found, but all conjuncts are required and the duplication/shared-constant failure decisively makes the criterion false.

The sole decimal column is `killbill_invoice_amount numeric(12, 2)`, the explicitly permitte

`server/services/cart.js` carries money through named `*_minor` values, computes each line as `unit_price_minor * quantity`, reduces integer line totals for subtotals, takes shipping from `price_minor`, calls `taxFor(goodsSubtotalMinor)`, and sums those values directly for `total_minor`.

`server/services/orders.js` independently re-prices from integer `price_minor`, computes goods subtotal and subtotal using integer multiplication/addition, gets shipping as integer `price_minor`, computes tax with `taxFor(goodsSubtotal)`, inserts all values into `*_minor` order fields, and stores each order-line total as `unit_price_minor * quantity`.

`server/money.js` implements 10% tax as `Math.trunc(Number(taxableSubtotalMinor) / 10)`, satisfying integer arithmetic truncated toward zero. Its `/ 100` operation occurs only inside `formatMinor` and `minorToDecimalString`, respectively display formatting and the permitted billing decimal conversion.

`server/killbill.js` derives the external invoice amount only via `minorToDecimalString(totalMinor)`, then sends that amount to Kill Bill; after invoicing, `server/services/orders.js` stores the returned decimal string only in `killbill_invoice_amount`.

Browser-island source also retains minor units: `src/islands/BuyPanel.jsx` formats `variant.price_minor`; `src/islands/CartLines.jsx` computes optimistic line totals as `line.unit_price_minor * qty` and formats all subtotal/shipping/tax/total `*_minor` fields. `src/lib/money.js` converts to dollars/cents only in `formatMinor` for display.

Targeted source searches across JavaScript found no `parseFloat`, money-related `parseInt`, `toFixed`, division by 100, or floating-rate multiplication in money code. The only JSX `toFixed` matches were unrelated visual animation/color values.
